title: LLM Inference Challenges - Understanding GPU Communication & Networking
author: Anurag Mohan

blocks.text: In the previous part, we explored distributed serving, replicas, request routing, schedulers, and how requests flow through large inference systems.
At this point, something important starts becoming visible.
A replica is not just:

one GPU
one machine
or one server
A replica may actually contain:

many GPUs
many servers
tensor parallel groups
pipeline stages
schedulers
KV cache systems
And all of these components must constantly communicate with each other.
That naturally leads to the next question.
Why does GPU communication matter so much?
Modern inference systems are highly distributed.
During inference:

GPUs exchange activations
tensor parallel GPUs combine partial outputs
pipeline stages pass intermediate tensors
KV cache updates happen continuously
schedulers coordinate batches
So communication is happening constantly.
And this communication can become a bottleneck very quickly.
Why can communication become a bottleneck?
Suppose computation is extremely fast.
But after every computation:

GPUs must wait for data
tensors must move across devices
synchronization must happen
Then eventually:

communication time
>
compute time
At that point:

GPUs sit idle waiting for data
utilization drops
latency increases
throughput suffers
So large-scale inference is not only about GPU compute anymore.
It is also about:

moving data efficiently
between GPUs
What kinds of communication happen during inference?
Different parallelism strategies create different communication patterns.
Tensor parallelism requires very frequent GPU communication.
Why?
Because multiple GPUs cooperate on the same layer.
Example:

GPU 1 → partial computation
GPU 2 → partial computation
GPU 3 → partial computation
GPU 4 → partial computation
Now their outputs must be combined.
This may happen:

after every attention block
after matrix multiplications
after intermediate activations
So tensor parallelism is extremely communication-heavy.
What about pipeline parallelism?
Pipeline parallelism communicates differently.
Here:

one stage finishes computation
then sends activations to the next stage
Example:
Stage 1 → Stage 2 → Stage 3 → Stage 4
So communication mainly happens:

between stages
during forward progression through the model
Compared to tensor parallelism:

communication frequency is usually lower
but transferred tensors may still be large
What about data parallelism?
Data parallelism is different.
During inference:

replicas are mostly independent
requests stay within one replica
communication between replicas is smaller
So inference-time data parallelism usually creates much less communication pressure.
Why is tensor parallelism often limited to one server?
Because tensor parallelism requires extremely fast communication.
Suppose GPUs must synchronize after nearly every operation.
If those GPUs are spread across slow networks:

latency increases heavily
synchronization becomes expensive
performance collapses
So systems often try to keep tensor parallel GPUs:
inside the same machine
where communication is fastest.
How do GPUs communicate inside one server?
Inside a server, GPUs often communicate using:

NVLink
or
NVSwitch
These are specialized high-speed GPU interconnects.
What is NVLink?
NVLink is a very high-speed communication link between GPUs.
Instead of:
GPU → CPU → GPU
NVLink allows:
GPU ↔ GPU
communication directly.
This provides:

much higher bandwidth
lower latency
faster synchronization
compared to normal PCIe communication.
Why is this important?
Suppose tensor parallel GPUs constantly exchange activations.
Without fast communication:

GPUs spend time waiting
synchronization slows down
throughput decreases
NVLink helps reduce that overhead.
This is one reason modern AI servers are designed heavily around:
GPU interconnect topology
not just raw GPU count.
What is NVSwitch?
NVSwitch extends this idea further.
Instead of direct links between only certain GPUs:

NVSwitch allows many GPUs to communicate efficiently together
almost like a high-speed GPU network switch
Example:
GPU 1 ↔ NVSwitch ↔ GPU 8
This becomes important in servers with:

8 GPUs
16 GPUs
or larger GPU configurations
What happens if one server is not enough?
Eventually models become too large.
Now:

one replica may span many servers
tensor parallel groups may cross machines
pipeline stages may live on different nodes
Now communication must happen:
across servers
This is called:
inter-node communication
At this point, what exactly is a replica then?
Honestly, this was one of the points that initially confused me while learning all this.
At first, I was thinking about replicas similar to traditional backend systems:

Load Balancer
   ↓
Server 1
Server 2
Server 3
where:

one endpoint maps to one server
and each server independently handles requests
But modern inference systems work very differently.
A replica is usually not just:

one GPU
one server
or one machine
Instead, a replica is closer to:
one distributed model-serving runtime
built using:

many GPUs
multiple servers
networking
schedulers
communication libraries
and inference software
For example, systems like:

vLLM
TGI
SGLang
TensorRT-LLM
coordinate many GPUs together and expose them logically as:
ONE serving endpoint
So internally, a replica may look like:

Server A → GPUs 1–8
Server B → GPUs 9–16
Server C → GPUs 17–24
Server D → GPUs 25–32
But externally:

Load Balancer
    ↓
Replica Endpoint
still behaves like one model-serving unit.
So the important mental shift becomes:

Replica
≠
one machine

Replica
=
software + distributed hardware
working together
as one logical inference system
And honestly, this is where inference systems start feeling much closer to distributed supercomputing systems than traditional backend applications.
Why is inter-node communication harder?
Because communication across servers is slower than communication inside one server.
Inside one machine:

GPUs may use NVLink
latency is extremely low
bandwidth is extremely high
Across machines:

data travels through network hardware
switches become involved
congestion may happen
latency increases
So distributed inference systems become highly dependent on networking quality.
What networking is commonly used between servers?
Large inference clusters often use:
InfiniBand
or advanced RDMA-capable networking.
These technologies are optimized for:

very high throughput
low latency
efficient GPU communication
What is RDMA?
RDMA means:
Remote Direct Memory Access
The important idea is:

one machine can access memory on another machine
with minimal CPU involvement
This helps reduce:

latency
CPU overhead
unnecessary memory copying
which becomes very important at scale.
Why does CPU involvement matter?
Suppose every GPU communication required:
GPU → CPU → Network → CPU → GPU
Then:

CPUs become bottlenecks
memory copying increases
latency grows significantly
RDMA helps communication happen more directly.
What is NCCL?
At this point another important component appears.
NCCL
pronounced:
Nickel
NCCL is NVIDIA’s communication library for multi-GPU systems.
It helps GPUs coordinate operations like:

synchronization
tensor exchange
reductions
collective communication
What are collective operations?
Suppose multiple GPUs each compute partial outputs.
Now they must combine results.
Example:

GPU 1 → partial tensor
GPU 2 → partial tensor
GPU 3 → partial tensor
GPU 4 → partial tensor
NCCL helps efficiently perform operations like:
combine everything together
across GPUs.
What is all-reduce?
One very common communication pattern is:
all-reduce
The idea is:

every GPU contributes data
data gets combined
every GPU receives the final combined result
This is heavily used in:

distributed training
tensor parallel inference
synchronization operations
Why do communication patterns matter so much?
Because at scale:

communication architecture
=
performance architecture
Two systems with:

the same GPUs
the same model
the same software
can still perform very differently depending on:

network topology
interconnect bandwidth
communication overhead
synchronization efficiency
What does a real cluster start looking like?
At this point, inference systems start looking less like normal backend systems.
And much more like:
distributed supercomputing systems
Because now we are coordinating:

hundreds of GPUs
across many servers
with high-speed networking
while maintaining low latency
and keeping utilization high
What is the key intuition?
Tensor parallelism creates:
heavy communication
Pipeline parallelism creates:
stage-to-stage communication
Data parallelism creates:
replicated serving systems
And networking becomes the foundation that allows all of this to function efficiently.
What becomes difficult at this stage?
Honestly, this is usually the stage where the mental model becomes harder.
Because now we are no longer only thinking about:

transformers
tensors
batching
inference loops
We are also thinking about:

cluster topology
GPU placement
networking hardware
synchronization overhead
distributed communication efficiency
And this is exactly why modern inference engineering starts overlapping heavily with:
distributed systems engineering
What comes next?
At this point, we now understand:

replicas
distributed serving
request routing
GPU communication
NVLink
NCCL
multi-node inference systems
And honestly, the mental model has now shifted quite a bit.
We are no longer thinking only about:

“running a model”
or “calling an API”
We are now thinking about:

distributed GPU systems
schedulers
communication bottlenecks
and large-scale inference infrastructure
But there is still one extremely important piece missing.
Even with all this infrastructure:

why does inference still become slow?
why are GPUs sometimes underutilized?
why is batching difficult during generation?
and why do serving systems behave very differently during prompt processing vs token generation?
This leads to one of the most important runtime concepts in inference systems:
Prefill vs Decode
In the next part, we will explore:

what prefill actually does
what decode actually does
why decode becomes sequential
why GPU utilization changes dramatically
why batching becomes difficult during generation
and why modern serving systems focus so heavily on scheduler design
Honestly, this is one of the key concepts needed before understanding:

continuous batching
paged attention
and vLLM internals
Because once prefill vs decode becomes intuitive, many modern inference optimizations suddenly start making much more sense.
